subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF LOTTERY FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Western grain farmers have amassed a jackpot of nearly $1 billion, and even though the Tories have told the Government to give it back to the farmers, the Government does not appear to know how to make a pay-out. Since the Government is determined to run lotteries, the agricultural reporter for the Calgary Herald, John Schmidt, has come up with a solution.
Since Liberal politicians are wringing their hands because they don't know what to do with the money, the trustees of the Chancellor War Memorial Hall in Bow River are suggesting that the $ 1 billion be sent to Chancellor and be put into a big pot called the Lotta Crow, that the 150,000 Wheat Board permit books also be shipped to Chancellor, and that a nationally televised draw could be made on April Fool's Day, by Otto Lang.
There would be 500 prizes of $1 million, and 1,000 prizes of $500,000. The grain growers could become so independently wealthy that the new Crow rates would never bother them at all. This could be the world's largest lottery pay-out and this Lotta Crow would be more exciting and create more publicity about the gamble of growing wheat than the small payment planned by the Government in the distant future. The trouble now is that the farmers keep paying into the fund, but the
Government uses every excuse in the book not to make a pay-out.
Don't you think, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers have a big enough gamble already, what with the weather, the grasshoppers, and this Liberal Government? Do we have to add another gamble for the farmers to get a pay-out?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR POLICY DETAILS CONCERNING USE OF ASBESTOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at a time when the use of asbestos is being thoroughly reviewed in the United States, an Ontario Royal Commission of Inquiry has now published a report that may worsen the situation considerably. Not only does the report fail to clarify the issue, it also raises a number of questions, including the fact that it is more dangerous to remove asbestos from buildings than to leave it in place.
On the other hand, in recent years the Government of the Province of Quebec, which owns two asbestos mines at Thet-ford Mines, and our own Government, have authorized and paid for programs to remove injected asbestos from certain buildings.
The four years of study and investigation required to prepare this report have produced only one result, which is to heighten and add to the controversy around the use of asbestos. This controversy, which has existed for a number of years, has had very tragic consequences for the producing region and thousands of workers. I may remind Hon. Members that these workers are just as concerned about their health as the rest of the country.
Mr. Speaker, in the circumstances, it is now imperative that our Government announce its official position on asbestos, in order to inform Canadians and Americans as well.
On behalf of the people working in the asbestos mines and on my own behalf, I say that we can and should use asbestos and can do so without risk. Now that the Government of Quebec has failed to clarify this issue-

May 8, 1984

subsubtopic: LOCATION FOR PROPOSED AGRICULTURAL LABORATORY IN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw a priority matter to the attention of the Government, and particularly to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). My statement is an earnest suggestion regarding the location of the $10 million Agriculture Canada laboratory which is proposed for southwestern Ontario. The County of Oxford will be most pleased to relieve the tension and indecision which the Members from London East, London West, and London-Mid-dlesex have displayed in prior discussions which had seemed to establish the site in the City of London.
As Oxford's Godfather, the Minister of Agriculture will be aware of the many attributes of Oxford pertaining to agriculture. Woodstock, the county seat, is known as the dairy capital of Canada, and many agriculture-related facilities are established within Oxford's boundaries, such as the Agriculture Campus of Fanshawe College, and the head office of the Ontario Flue Cured Tobocco Growers' Marketing Board. Its geographical location, just a few kilometres from the University of Western Ontario, and equidistant from Toronto and Windsor, would seem to indicate that I am offering an ideal site for this project.
I would also suggest that an acceptance of this proposal to establish a laboratory in Oxford would confirm the Government's expressed impartiality when locating projects of this magnitude.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGENCIES AND ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recommendation of the Flouse of Commons Committee on Visible Minorities that the proposed Ministry of Multiculturalism should provide increased and extended funding to ethnic groups and broadly-based community organizations, has received strong support from many such groups.
A number of organizations now serving immigrants receive assistance from the Department of Employment and Immigration under ISAP, the Immigrant Settlement and Adaptation Program. The Ontario Council of Agencies Serving Immigrants speaks for many in voicing its concern that the Department of Employment and Immigration is contemplating a redistribution of the ISAP budget to tie ISAP assistance to intake of new immigrants, without regard to the question of continuing to meet the needs of existing immigrants. These agencies and organizations are hard-pressed to remain in existence, and any effective reduction in their funding is indeed cause for concern.
Until funds are available from another source, such as the proposed Ministry of Multiculturalism, I trust the Department of Employment and Immigration will not take any steps which would have the effect of lowering existing levels of assistance to agencies or organizations serving the immigrant community.

subsubtopic: NEEDS OF IMMIGRANT CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in major cities across the country, including Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, and Vancouver, a substantial and growing percentage of students attending schools come from families in which the language spoken at home is neither English nor French. These children are attending schools in Canada because the immigration policies of the federal Government in recent years have permitted and encouraged their parents to come to this country. It is now becoming increasingly evident to teachers, parents, and community groups that problems are developing for these students because they are not getting the services they need. They require assistance in order that they can fit into Canadian life on an equivalent basis with young people born in Canada.
Equality Now, the report of the Special Committee on Visible Minorities in Canadian Society, made a series of very good recommendations urging the federal Government, through the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal), to encourage provincial Governments and school boards to develop and implement policies to improve race relations. The provinces, which are responsible for education, are finding it increasingly difficult to provide local educational systems with sufficient funding to meet those special needs.
I urge the Secretary of State to give consideration to the federal Government sharing the cost to the provinces of funding to meet the needs of immigrant children in Canada, considering that this may be the only possibility which would allow these services to be provided.

subsubtopic: ADDITIONAL ICE BREAKING SERVICES SOUGHT FOR NEWFOUNDLAND REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of the House the great need for better ice breaking services along the coastline of Newfoundland. I checked today and I discovered that only one of the four ice-breakers assigned to the Newfoundland region is presently operative. We have two new ice-breakers coming on stream shortly which have been assigned to the western region, to Vancouver.
May 8, 1984

The Maritime region has no problems; it has lots of icebreakers. The Quebec region has no problems; it has lots of ice-breakers. However, on my coastline there are boats stuck in port with people out of work because of that, ferry systems to four islands are cut off most of the wintertime, large ships are unable to get into port, and 11 long-liners have been stuck for the past 37 days, with 60 men aboard. I do not think this is good enough. I ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) to intervene to give the Newfoundland region more ice-breaker services on a permanent basis.

subsubtopic: RAPE CONVICTION SENTENCES-CALL FOR APPEAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in October last year in Hall Beach, Northwest Territories, three adult men took a 13-year old Inuit girl to the home of one of them. All three had sexual intercourse with her, as a result of which she became pregnant.
The crime which was committed is viewed by Parliament as a most serious one, and one for which Parliament has prescribed a maximum penalty of life imprisonment. However, on April 21 the convicted persons were sentenced to only one week in jail each, of which only a few days were actually served. So light a sentence almost condones the criminal behaviour of the guilty parties. The public of the Northwest Territories, especially those organizations representing native women, are outraged, as am I, at what can only be described as a miscarriage of justice.
The sentence of the court must be appealed so that confidence in the administration of justice and the court system be maintained. The law ought to be applied equitably and fairly without regard to race, and a sentence of only one week's imprisonment for what is commonly referred to as statutory rape ought not to be allowed to stand.

subsubtopic: ATTENDANCE DURING ADDRESS BY PRESIDENT OF MEXICO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was indeed an honour and a privilege to sit in this Assembly earlier this day to hear the President of Mexico, His Excellency Mr. de la Madrid, address this Assembly, the nation, and indeed the world. This was an historic event.
The President's message was important and laid guideposts and stepping stones on the road toward more harmonious relations within and between the nations of the two American continents. What was not so pleasant was the extent to which chairs in the Assembly were empty during the President's remarks. Even more disrespectful was the late entry of many
Oral Questions
Members into the Assembly. In my view the honour, dignity, and pride of this Assembly trembled today.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: STATISTICS CANADA ANALYSIS-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO HELP UNEMPLOYED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance, I would like to direct my question to the Prime Minister. As reported in Hansard of April 6, 1984, the Minister of Finance stated the following at that time:
-we expect the unemployment rate to fall during the course of this year. I still expect this to happen, and I am not considering at the present time making any changes to the Budget-
Yesterday Statistics Canada reported in its economic analysis that there is a slackening of employment growth and that, because of the slowing down of the recovery in the United States, the rate of recovery in Canada may not be sufficient to reduce unemployment substantially in the first half of the year.
In view of the fact that the Minister's forecast is again incorrect in that unemployment rates are higher than he forecast, and the Statistics Canada forecast is even worse, will the Prime Minister direct the Minister to bring in a new Budget containing some changes to help the 1,541,000 people here in Canada who are unemployed? The Prime Minister is a lame duck, and he is now raising his wing toward the Minister of Finance.

subsubtopic: STATISTICS CANADA ANALYSIS-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO HELP UNEMPLOYED

subsubtopic: STATISTICS CANADA ANALYSIS-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO HELP UNEMPLOYED
speechtext: Bring them in now.

subsubtopic: STATISTICS CANADA ANALYSIS-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO HELP UNEMPLOYED
speechtext: Oh, oh!

May 8, 1984
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: STATISTICS CANADA ANALYSIS-REQUEST FOR NEW BUDGET TO HELP UNEMPLOYED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on February 17, 1984, the Minister of Finance said that his new Budget is not having any effect on the Canadian economy and that that makes him happy. How can legislation stemming from the new Budget have any effect on the economy if the Minister has already said that the Budget has had no effect on the economy? So much for his legislation.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: INTEREST RATES CHARGED BY CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Today the chartered banks have increased the prime bank rate to 12 per cent. In the United States, banks have raised interest rates to 12.5 per cent. So much for Mr. Kaufman's forecast. He is 100 per cent more accurate than the Minister of Finance. Given these increases in interest rates, what action will the Minister now take to try to get the economic recovery moving along again here in Canada?

subsubtopic: INTEREST RATES CHARGED BY CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, not only do Members of the Opposition display their ignorance, they are also intellectually dishonest in their analysis of the situation and the statements which have been made. I never said that my Budget would not have any impact on the economy. What I did say was that the Budget was aimed at sustaining the basic trend of the economy which was in full recovery after last year's April Budget, I mean a stable and continuing growing trend in the coming months. The latest Figures made public seem to indicate that indeed we have achieved that stable and continuing growth to which I referred in my Budget.
As to the increase in interest rates, the Hon. Member knows for instance that the bank prime rate went up half a percentage point in the United States today, up from 12 to 12.5 per cent in most American banks. It was inevitable and understandable that certain Canadian banks would raise their prime rate, to 12 per cent in this case, which still leaves Canadian interest rates half a percentage point lower than what they are now in the United States.
Personally, I deplore this latest increase in interest rates, particularly in the United States. That does not leave us the choice to keep our rates much lower than those now prevailing. This concern is shared by most industrialized nations and their Ministers of Finance whom I met with recently. We will have another opportunity to discuss this issue at next week's OECD meeting which will be attended by American Government officials, of course. Together we will try to see whether there is any possibility of finding ways to reduce interest rates, or at least prevent them from rising even more.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the OECD will not need the Minister for his forecasting ability.
On March 12 the Minister said, and I quote from the Ottawa Citizen:
Interest rates will remain stable for most of 1984 and drop towards the end of
the year.
Interest rates have gone up one percentage point since. So much for the forecasting ability of the Minister or for his scrupulous truthfulness.
How can anyone in Canada, whether an economist or other citizen, have any confidence in the Minister after he has made these consistently wrong forecasts just weeks before interest rates go up, unemployment goes up, and the Minister promises they will go down? How often can the Minister cry wolf without Canadians being completely gobbled up? How long is the Minister going to continue in his portfolio after this astounding display of incompetence?

Mr. Speaker, I have taken extra care to mention every time I have spoken on this subject that the forecasts were what they were, that is, they were an estimation of what might happen in the economy at a particular time. I have indicated many times that they should be seen as such. They were estimations of what could happen and the evidence is systematic-
We cannot believe a word you say.
-including the forecasts when the Hon. Member was Minister of Finance. The fact is that the world economy usually develops in a different way than most forecasts, anyway.
Resign now!
I can show to the Hon. Member-
Do you have his resignation, Mr. Prime Minister?

I can show to the Hon. Member, for instance, that last year Canada knew a rate of inflation which was lower than the one I had forecast, and a rate of job creation which was higher than I had forecast-
Tell the unemployed.

-and we knew a rate of growth in the Canadian economy in 1983 which was higher than the one I forecast in my Budget. Therefore, sometimes in those forecasts you will have results which are better than those you have anticipated, and sometimes they will be worse than you have anticipated. What anyone must do is try to work on the basis of the best advice you can get in that regard.
May 8, 1984
You are a travesty.

I refer my friend to the forecasts which have been made internationally, and those which have been made by dozens of national agencies in the private sector, and he will find out that the forecasts made by myself as Minister of Finance are very much in line with the average forecasts made in the private sector of the Canadian economy.
God help the OECD.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INFORMATION REGARDING FUTURE OF HOUSING CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always rather fascinated by the remarks made by the Minister of Finance, to whom I would like to direct a question about what he has done and what he intends to do in the months to come, considering the problems Canadians will be facing as a result of high interest rates.
As far as the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation is concerned, the Minister of Finance is aware that in recent months there were over 27,000 fewer housing starts than during the last three months of last year. The person responsible for statistics at the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation is very concerned about the effect high interest rates will have on the construction industry. Does the Minister of Finance have any suggestions he might like to make to the House for avoiding the same problems this vital sector of our economy was experiencing only two years ago?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INFORMATION REGARDING FUTURE OF HOUSING CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad the Hon. Member raised this point. I may remind him that according to the forecast, this year the number of housing units built in Canada will increase at a higher rate than it did last year. We expect that between 160,000 and 170,000 housing units will be built this year.
The Hon. Member may recall that early last year, a number of federal and provincial programs aimed at stimulating construction were operational at a time when we had experienced a very substantial slow-down in the Canadian economy.
Since the Hon. Member is asking whether we have any measures in mind, I would like to ask him, as soon as the Bill is introduced at the end of May, to support our measures to provide insurance against rising interest rates for homeowners with mortgages. I also invite the Hon. Member to support the amendments we shall be proposing to the Interest Act, to ensure that borrowers will be able to pay off their mortgages early if they decide it would be to their advantage to do so.
Oral Questions
These measures were announced in the Budget and will be introduced in the House in the form of legislation at the end of May. I hope we shall have the co-operation of the Opposition so that these measures can then be adopted forthwith.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary. I certainly would like to accept the Minister's invitation. However, he said that his projections would give us 160,000 more housing starts, but according to the results for February, March and April, we have had 26,000 fewer housing starts than last year. Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will understand that the Canadian people may have some doubts about the Minister's projections.
In the circumstances, I would ask the Minister, since he referred to his mortgage insurance program, what the maximum would be for insured rates? That is the kind of information we must have as soon as possible if we want to prevent the recession in the construction industry from getting worse. In the circumstances, I would like to invite the Minister to introduce his Bill as soon as possible, because of the drop in housing starts in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have two things to say to the Hon. Member. The First one is that last year, there was a rise in housing construction during the first few months of the year because we had a home ownership stimulation plan that expired at the beginning of the year. Later on, there was a slow-down in the construction industry. This year, we seem to be seeing the reverse, since we had a slow-down in the construction industry at the beginning of the year, and now we hope and we believe that construction will pick up in the months to come, in 1984. That is why we expect to see at least as many housing units this year as last year.
Second, as far as the Mortgage Rate Protection Program is concerned, I must say the Opposition's homework is pretty hopeless. The Hon. Member asked me what the insured rate would be. I indicated this in my Budget. I also tabled in the House a paper providing all the details of this program, and I would invite the Hon. Member to read this paper. He would realize that the program provides insurance and security for both mortgagees and mortgagors, that the program is quite clear and provides the assurances the Hon. Member is seeking.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER OF CORPORATE MERGERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is appropriate to give credit where credit is due. As a result of government policy we have seen considerable econom-

May 8, 1984
Oral Questions
ic activity in a certain sector, namely, the corporate takeover and merger sector. Corporate mergers in 1983 were higher than they had ever been in Canadian history. Because this is occurring largely as a result of government policy, I ask the Minister of Finance what benefits do average Canadian citizens receive as a result of government policy which encourages and rewards corporate takeovers and mergers?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER OF CORPORATE MERGERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have taken steps over the years to ensure that the takeovers and mergers are not going to be detrimental to the Canadian people. We have done this, first of all by ensuring that foreign takeovers are controlled. Contrary to the view of the Conservative Party which would like to do away with the protection we have for Canadian industry and ownership, we have taken steps to maintain the existence of control of foreign ownership in this country. The Hon. Member knows what the Leader of the Opposition has said in that regard where, for all practical purposes, he would do away with that kind of control of Canadian ownership in this country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER OF CORPORATE MERGERS
speechtext: You had better check with John Turner.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER OF CORPORATE MERGERS
speechtext: With regard to takeovers and mergers, the Hon. Member knows that this process is occurring all the time in a free economy. This is a normal process. There are laws under the Competition Act to prevent undue detrimental impact on the Canadian public. My colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, has introduced a Bill for which she has asked early consideration. This Bill will provide for additional measures in that regard. Again I invite the Opposition to take note of the Bills before the House, to give them support, and to ensure that we have laws on the books which are completely adapted to the needs of today.

Mr. Speaker, although that answer was very elaborate, I would like to repeat my original question. The Government of Canada has tax legislation which encourages and rewards corporate takeovers and mergers. In other words, it makes it an attractive process. How do mergers and takeovers assist Canadians? In other words, government policy which encourages this must be in place because it is going to have an over-all benefit to Canadians. How do Canadians benefit from corporate takeovers?

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to say that, contrary to what the Hon. Member has said, we do not have a fiscal or taxation policy which favours or encourages takeovers or mergers. We are trying to establish a policy which is neutral in that regard and will not favour or discourage takeovers or mergers.
As far as the question raised by the Hon. Member is concerned, I think we will have to spend time on a first year course in economics. Surely he has heard about rationalization in the industry whereby firms are merging, or are taken over,
in order to become more efficient and competitive in world markets. That is how large firms have been built which, in Canada or other countries, are carrying on large shares of the export market and world trade today. You are not going to take over a large share of the world trade if you continue with corner shop operations. You must have large units which are able to compete in world markets. Surely my hon. friend knows that.
Mr. Speaker, surely the Minister of Finance's hon. friend does not know that.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote to the Minister of Finance from Mr. McKinley of the Combines Branch of his own Government.
Order. On a second supplementary question, quotations from documents should be absolutely minimal.

Mr. Speaker, I will not quote from the document. However, officials in his Government suggest that there is no evidence to suggest that the economies of scale that result from corporate takeovers have benefited Canadian society. A major report coming from the United States suggested that, out of 200 reasons that corporate managers have for corporate takeovers, economies of scale rank 198 out of 200.
Based on evidence available which indicates that corporate takeovers do not result in net benefit to Canadian citizens, why does the Minister keep tax legislation in place which encourages and rewards this kind of economic behaviour, this paper shuffling, as opposed to real job creation and economic development?

Mr. Speaker, I already answered this question when I clearly stated that our fiscal legislation neither favours nor promotes corporate takeovers or mergers, but that its objective is to establish a policy which is neutral, allowing the marketplace to decide whether it would benefit from a particular corporate takeover or merger. There is, however, in our tax legislation no provision which would systematically favour or promote corporate takeovers or mergers. We try to make our system as neutral as possible.

subsubtopic: MORTGAGE RATE PROTECTION PROGRAM-TIMING OF APPLICATION TO MORTGAGE RENEWALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The details of the Mortgage Rate Protection Program in the budget papers state:
The interest rate to be protected will be the market interest rate prevailing for the relevant mortgage term at the time the mortgage protection is taken out.
May 8, 1984

The Government has delayed the introduction of this legislation for almost two months, and interest rates have gone up almost 2 per cent. Will the Minister admit to the House that his Department is misleading the Canadian people when it suggests, as it did on the telephone today, that the insurance will be available at the rate at which the mortgage is taken out or renewed, rather than the rate at the time the application is approved?

subsubtopic: MORTGAGE RATE PROTECTION PROGRAM-TIMING OF APPLICATION TO MORTGAGE RENEWALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I told the Hon. Member yesterday that he would have to wait until the bill is introduced in the House. Then, he will be able to find out for himself what legislative provisions are taken in that respect.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the Minister that people who are renewing mortgages want the truth from the Department now. Each day's delay in bringing in that legislation is affecting housing starts, which are dropping. Each delayed housing start costs Canada's housing industry two and one-half jobs. Each day's delay, while mortgage interest rates rise, costs Canadian home owners. On March 20 the Minister said a few weeks. Last week the Minister said the end of May. Why is the Minister delaying in bringing in that legislation?

Mr. Speaker, I answered this question yesterday. I indicated that we had extensive consultations with all the private sector people and organizations in this regard to ensure that the Bill which would be introduced would be a piece of legislation which would address the situation appropriately and would meet the needs of all parties concerned. We have concluded those discussions and are in the process of finalizing the drafting of the Bill.
I am happy to see that, for once, the Opposition will co-operate when this Bill is introduced. I am looking forward to seeing this happen because there are now five or six financial Bills before this House which would be beneficial to Canadian citizens and Canadian industry.
Bring them forth.

They are before the House at the present time and the Conservatives have reneged on an agreement to pass those Bills expeditiously. That is what the Conservatives have been doing in this place.
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: IDENTITY OF GUNMAN INVOLVED IN QUEBEC NATIONAL ASSEMBLY INCIDENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Defence. Can the Minister of Defence confirm that the gunman involved in the very distressing situation at the Quebec national Assembly is in fact a member of the Canadian Armed Forces, and is a member of the security detail attached to the government bunker at Carp near Ottawa?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to join with you and other Members of the House who offer their condolences and express their views relating to this tragedy.
As I understand it, the gunman has now been captured and is in the custody of the QPP. My information is that he is a member of the Canadian Forces. However, I do not have details relating to the unit. I cannot confirm the unit to which he belongs at this time.
speakername: Hon.   J.-J. Blais@Minister of National Defence

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we certainly join with the Minister in offering condolences to those who lost family and those who were injured in that most unfortunate incident.
I realize it is a very short time after the event. However, I would like to ask the Minister whether he can advise the House how it was possible for a private soldier to get a semi-automatic or automatic rifle from the armouries, with ammunition, which is guarded quite carefully. What kind of security checks are made to determine the mental stability of individuals who are responsible for protecting the Cabinet, Cabinet facilities, and the ultra secret equipment that is a component of that important part of our emergency measures operation? [ Translation]

Member that we are well aware that military personnel have access to weapons of war which by their very nature are dangerous, and that we are taking every necessary precaution to ensure that the people who are using these weapons are mentally stable people. May 8, 1984
Oral Questions
speakername: Hon.   J.-J. Blais@Minister of National Defence

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN CORPORATE EXECUTIVES' SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. I am sure that the Minister knows that in recent years the average increase in wages and salaries for most Canadians ran behind the increase in the cost of living. Last year the average increase in wages and salaries was more than one per cent less than the increase in the cost of living. This is partly because of the recession, and partly because of the kind of lecturing that the Minister has given to Canadians, urging them to show restraint.
Yesterday we were given the news that Canadian executive salaries jumped last year by 12.5 per cent. Dome Petroleum increased them by 42 per cent, Genstar by 86 per cent, and McIntyre Mines by 71 per cent. I suppose it is too much to ask the Minister to plug some of the loopholes in the Income Tax Act, but may I ask him if he could make a speech in the next while urging Canadian executives to show the same kind of restraint that he has asked Canadian workers to show?

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN CORPORATE EXECUTIVES' SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, contrary to what the Hon. Member has said, over the last several years the average increase in wages has been higher than the cost of living. I invite my friend to look at the figures, both in terms of the average salaries and in terms of the disposable income, which is the income after taxes. He will find that, as an average over the last several years, increases have been higher than the cost of living, not lower.
As far as executive salaries are concerned, he mentioned a few specific cases. Obviously I do not have the detailed information on individual firms, but I will be pleased to send him copies of the speeches I have made already on this very subject that have, indeed urged management in the firms to ensure that increases in their level of renumeration were showing the same restraint in line with the restraint that we were asking of workers. I have stated quite categorically that it would indeed be extremely counterproductive and prejudicial if increases in senior management renumeration were to exceed those that they were ready to concede to their workers in general.
I will be happy to repeat those admonitions at any opportunity that I have. I can take this opportunity today to appeal to senior executives to make sure that they will show the same kind of restraint that they are asking their workers to show during these difficult times. I would hope that indeed we will see that average increases like the ones mentioned by the Hon. Member are not happening as a rule among Canadian industries.

Mr. Speaker, Dome Petroleum continues to function as a company today thanks to
the bank loans which were guaranteed by the Government. Yet in 1983, Dome, a company which is close to floating in red ink, gave its executive officers a 42 per cent increase in salary and benefits. Does the Minister believe that such extravagance by a government supported corporation is justified and, if not, what is the Government prepared to do to see that executives in Dome and other corporations bring their salaries into line?

The House resumed from Monday, May 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet (for Mr. Gray) that Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we are debating the federal Government's Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof. In essence, the Bill recognizes belatedly that the Government has lost control over the hundreds of Crown corporations which it operates. Indeed, some months ago, when asked how many Crown corporations the Government had, the then President of the Treasury Board was unable to answer that question even to the nearest hundred. As it turns out, the Government in fact owns and operates some 500 Crown corporations.
Those companies vary greatly in size. On the one hand there are the huge conglomerates like Canadian National, Air Canada and the CBC which employ thousands of people. On the other hand there are those like the Canadian Saltfish Corporation, which in the private sector would be viewed as a small business, employing somewhere in the vicinity of a dozen to a couple of hundred people. Together, whatever the size of the company, government Crown corporations constitute such a large part of the economy that the Auditor General has
termed them a sub-government, rivalling the Government itself in economic might and impact. The truth is that under the present Government Crown corporations have been allowed to multiply like rabbits and grow like elephants. They are all but out of control.
It is bad enough that there are as many Crown corporations as there are, for all the good many of them do, but many have given rise to the creation of others, often without any authority to do so beyond themselves. Certainly Parliament has little control over their activities, a fact of growing concern to the Auditor General and to many Hon. Members of this Chamber. Now like the proverbial deathbed repentant, the Government has introduced this Bill in an effort to blunt swelling criticism about its lack of action.
Specifically, the Bill seeks to tighten control over Crown corporations by giving the Auditor General the authority he has sought. Moreover, henceforth Parliament will be required to approve the creation and operation of Crown corporations, and more information will be required concerning these companies. In the final analysis, however welcome may be the reforms in question, the Bill merely scratches the surface in holding Crown corporations to account. The legislation gives the appearance of action without delivering any genuine solution.
It is ironic that at the very time the Government was heralding Bill C-24, The Globe and Mail, Canada's national newspaper, was releasing confidential Cabinet documentation making it clear that de Havilland Aircraft of Canada Limited, a granddaddy of Crown corporations if ever there was one, will require hundreds of millions of dollars more in government subventions in the years ahead. Even with such support from the taxpayer, however, the principal product of the company, the Dash-8, is not expected to be marketable unless all kinds of questionable conditions prevail. For example, according to the confidential Cabinet document, interest rates will have to be very low and certainly much lower than they are now. The relevant unions at de Havilland will have to be prepared to accept generous wage concessions that in many instances they will not likely accept. Elowever, we are puzzled that the Government would announce to the country in March that it was prepared to bail out Canadair by assuming $1.5 billion in debt accumulated by that company through sheer bad management after the plane manufacturer had reported a loss of something like $540 million in 1983 alone.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join with my colleagues in opposing this legislation because it is simply inappropriate for the times. If the Government wanted to introduce a Bill which would have Opposition support, it should have introduced the former Bill C-27 which was authored by the Hon. Member for Welling-ton-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty). That Bill offered real accountability.
Financial Administration Act

We are discussing an area of public life which will affect us for many, many years into the future and one which will affect individual Canadians dramatically. It is a place in which we may debate the issues. The opinions of both sides are revealed in this place and out of that comes a collective wisdom that is better for the country. Once again, it is a case of the Cabinet making a decision and the individual Members not performing what in my submission is their responsibility as imposed upon them by their constituents.
I always find it wise to go back and look at an issue in its historic context. In the development of Crown corporations, there was a period of time that was known as the infrastructure period and this occurred from about the year 1800 to the year 1930. For 130 years the Government was involved in Crown corporations which dealt with ports, new harbour commissions, a few canals and the CNR. For 130 years those were essentially the only Crown corporations that existed.
After the restrictions and cutbacks caused by the Depression, a few more Crown corporations were formed. For example, the Bank of Canada, a farm loan board, the Canadian Wheat Board and the CBC were set up during that time in response to national sentiments and to counteract actions taken by the Government of the United States.
One might describe the third phase of Crown corporations as the war phase. At that time, the Hon. C. D. Howe set up numerous Crown corporations in order to cope with the demands of war. As well, those corporations were set up in part to avoid bureaucracy during the war and to attract managers who worked as the one-dollar-a-year type of manager. You will probably recall those events, Mr. Speaker. During the war phase, the strategic area of atomic energy was nationalized as well.
During the 1950s and the 1960s, a few Crown corporations were set up, most of which acted in the interests of patriotism. Such Crown corporations as the Canada Council, the CBC reorganization and Expo 67 were set up at that time. I suppose that from 1800 to about 1970 there was a maximum of about 50 or 60 Crown corporations in existence.
Since 1968 we have entered a new phase in the growth of Crown corporations. We have entered a phase of an absolute proliferation of Crown corporations which has given the Government and its executive control over broad areas of our society. I believe we should describe this phase as the socialist phase, and I mean socialist in terms of economics. I do not see socialism existing only in terms of social areas. I have no problem with having us collectively agree that we want to fund schools or hospitals publicly. However, when we start to move into the creation of wealth and the economic side of society and begin to nationalize and socialize through Crown corporations, that is when we become inefficient and block the natural

May 8, 1984
Financial Administration Act
market price signals which cause appropriate change where necessary. That is the problem with socialism and that is what has happened since 1972. There has been almost unlimited growth of marketing boards and nationalization of industries, under which Canadair and de Havilland fall. We have the situation of public servants going out and incorporating companies on their own, without even the Minister of the Department being aware of what they are doing; but the taxpayers have to jump in and get those companies off the hook. There is an example of this in British Columbia and it cost taxpayers something like $750 million.
Every few years Parliament has to write off $400 million, $500 million, $600 million or $700 million for the CNR. Air Canada, which is a well-run company, gets all sorts of privileges. When a company becomes an agent of Her Majesty, it can then obtain money more cheaply than private competitors can obtain it in the marketplace. Air Canada also has a monopoly. While it is well run , it is only succeeding because it still has some 5 per cent debentures in its annual report, and it has an absolute monopoly of many of the major points across the country, including the setting of rates. Therefore, it surely should succeed when it has that type of advantage. We might look at the Dungarvin Forest Service Company, which was set up under B.C. law. That company went belly-up and cost the taxpayers $750 million.	'
All of these Crown corporations-and there are over 400, including the subsidiaries-have the effect of distorting the marketplace. I know that my friends in the NDP dislike this profit motive and the concept of the invisible hand of Adam Smith. Adam Smith did not create the law. He was simply describing the phenomenon that if we do not change the times, and if we do not adopt new technology when our competitors do, the competitor will be able to provide a service to the public at a cheaper cost, and that service will be bought. If we do not change, we will go down.
That principle applies whether in a socialist country, a communist country, or here in Canada. We have not been prepared to face the changes that have occurred in the world. It is as if South Korea does not exist. That has been the public policy of this country. It is as if Japan has not come on. There seems to be a reluctance on the part of the Government to realize that we have to compete in the world and to make that case with Canadians, so that we can adopt high technology and change our educational system. That is what the invisible hand of Adam Smith is. He simply described, as did other scientists, the law of gravity. We might not like the law of gravity, but we still are faced with it as a reality. That is the invisible hand that Adam Smith described. We must always in public policy keep on the cutting edge.
Crown corporations, by virtue of being creatures of government and without the discipline of the marketplace, never fail. For example, we know that if 100 private companies are set up, at least 40 per cent of them will fail, either because of under-capitalization or inefficient management. But, Mr. Speaker, have you ever seen one Crown corporation fail? Never, Mr. Speaker; they simply come back and ask the taxpayers to kick in the money. That is the problem.
When Crown corporations are set up, they should be told: "Here is your mandate; either you make it or you die". I could live with that. But when Crown corporations continuously survive as a result of the infusion of public moneys, I take issue with that and I object to that. Those public moneys are coming out of the pockets of our mothers, fathers, sisters and brothers-taxpayers who are having a very difficult time meeting their mortgage payments and properly educating their children. I disagree with digging deeper into people's pockets to save a Crown corporation.
The reason we are saving Crown corporations is that if the Minister responsible sets a corporation up and that corporation fails, it affects the perception and success of the Minister. Therefore, he will not let that corporation fail. That has been the traditional response of government. When a government sets up a Crown corporation, it ensures that that corporation will succeed even if it takes every cent from every Canadian because it is the reputation of the government or the Minister which is at stake. We must cut through that.
This Bill is purported by the Government to give better accountability. When one looks behind it, in fact it does not perform that duty. I say to my colleagues opposite that they should adopt Bill C-27 which was presented during the Government of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) in 1979. That Bill was vastly superior in terms of accountability and setting forth the duties of directors.
When the Cabinet appoints a chief executive officer, the directors are nothing but an advisory, honorific body-a way to transfer money to more government supporters across the country. There should be a statute which puts the responsibility on the board of directors. They should hire the chief executive officer and monitor that chief executive officer day by day. If he does not cut the mustard, they can fire him because it would be their responsibility in law. Even that one change would be a major advance.

During my public career I have never been persuaded that the requirements for good financial management and control in Government need to differ at all when compared to those in any other corporation in the country, with one exception. I believe management and control over government corporations should be more stringent, because governments are dealing with what I regard as trust funds provided to them by the taxpayers of Canada to finance operations, whereas in the private sector, many times shareholders put up their own money knowing very well that they face a major risk when so doing.
When I look at the wording of Bill C-24, I can come to only one conclusion, namely, that it is a crass attempt to defuse the Crown corporations issue. In other words, it is simply a political exercise. I cannot believe in all sincerity that the Government would want this Bill to become law. It is simply too full of fundamental defects.
Bill C-24 covers some 183 Crown corporations and subsidiaries wholly owned by the federal Government. However, with all of this magician's hocus-pocus, this waving of the magic wand and holding up of a sheet, Parliament will still see only summaries of corporate plans, operating budgets and capital budgets as they are tabled by the appropriate Ministers. Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act dealing with the whole subject of the accountability of Crown corporations.
I welcome this opportunity because of the importance of the subject. First of all, it is important simply because of the sheer bulk of Crown corporations in our economy and in our daily lives. Both provincial and federal Crown corporations affect the daily lives of people in all parts of Canada, and there is widespread concern that there is neither financial nor social accountability built into these Crown corporations. Unlike private corporations which exist primarily to make a profit for their shareholders, Crown corporations are supposed to serve a public purpose. The public purpose, as we all know, can be defined in several different ways.
I was interested to read the remarks of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) regarding this Bill when he introduced it in March. He talked about the creation of the CNR by the Conservative Government in 1919, and about that he said, and I quote:
The objectives were to safeguard the Government's large investment in the railways, to protect Canada's image in foreign capital markets, and to avoid potential damage to large segments of the Canadian economy if the three companies (then on the brink of bankruptcy) did not continue to operate.
Beneath those very nice phrases, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that the accumulated companies which were brought into the CNR had accumulated debts of something like $1.3 billion. Through the Act which incorporated the CNR, not one investor lost any of that money, even though they had been investing in worthless stock, in effect. Therefore, basically what was defined as the "public purpose" at that time was to protect the investment community which had been speculating and had
made some very handsome profits out of Canadian lands and grants.
The Canadian National Railways was formed to protect its interests and not the public interest. However, at least today it is publicly owned and it could be made to conform with public policy. The concern of our Party is that the CNR and all Crown corporations should be made to conform with public policy in the largest sense of the word. This does not always happen. For example, Canadian National owns property in the Cowichan Estuary, Lot 160. It is presently involved in some major development on that land which will have a detrimental effect on the estuary and its ability to serve as a fish habitat. When we talk about public accountability, we want to see the broadest kind of accountability whereby Crown corporations will serve not just to earn money or provide transportation, as in the case of the CNR, but also to serve the public interest; in this case to protect the fish habitat. But we are having a great deal of difficulty finding out exactly what CNR's plans are for that area because they are very secretive. We believe that at the very least a Crown corporation, when possible, should be open to public scrutiny. There is absolutely no reason, in this particular case, why they could not be open.
We have a similar situation where the CNR is involved in double-tracking through Indian lands. Again, Indian people are having difficulty finding out exactly what is happening. Therefore, we say it is simply not enough that the CNR was nationalized; we would like to see it socialized as well. We would like to see the corporation serve community interests. Basically, we are concerned that this Bill does not help very much in moving in that direction.
There are many similar examples, and I have a very striking one in Petro-Canada. That corporation is involved in exploration in the area which the Lubicon Lake Band of northern Alberta is claiming. Last December the task force on the churches and corporate responsibility wrote a letter to the Chairman of Petro-Canada Exploration Inc., Mr. Albert Hopper, and I quote from that letter:
We have recently received reports that your Company and others are engaged in exploration, production and development on lands claimed by the Lubicon Lake Band. We understand that this industrial activity is proceeding despite the fact that the ownership of land is in dispute. Moreover, this activity apparently causes irreparable damage to the Band's way of life and livelihood and hence to its cohesion and its ability to survive as a band.
The letter goes on to ask a number of questions:
(1)	Has your company adopted certain principles governing its concepts of corporate responsibility?
(2)	Do these principles pertain to the impact of your company's activity on the social well being of people in areas of your operation?
(3)	What factors have influenced your Company's understanding of its corporate responsibility when faced with the plight of the Lubicon Band?
Would your Company accept the proposition that its corporate responsibility goes beyond what are strictly legal or regulatory requirements and accept, as many other companies do, a responsibility towards predicaments similar to those of the Lubicon Band?
(4)	Would you comment on the charges that the activity of your Company (and others) has the effect of causing irreparable damage to the hunting, trapping and fishing economy of the Lubicon Band? Could you tell us what
May 8, 1984

efforts your Company is making to minimize this damage so as not to destroy the Lubicon Band's sources of livelihood?
(5)	A Globe and Mail article (18 November 1983) states that the Band's legal costs are financed through a bank loan. Should your Company and others press to have the court costs assigned to the Band, the Band's diminished resources might make it impossible for it to appeal the court's decision.
Would your Company contemplate such a step, or would it expedite an appeal to a higher court as a necessary part of a multi-faceted process through which it will be determined if the claims of the Lubicon Band have just cause?
The response from Petro-Canada was very legalistic and did not deal with the substance of the questions that were asked. In other words, Petro-Canada does not wish to be brought to the bar of social responsibility and have to face up to questions about social responsibility.
We have to ask whether that kind of action on the part of Petro-Canada really serves the public interest. We in this Party believe that Crown corporations can serve a very positive role in the economy and in society. Generally we support them but we want to see financial and social accountability built in.
I was rather interested to hear the Conservative Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) talk about his concern that Crown corporations wanted to create wealth by using some of our natural resources and that this wealth would be used to finance social services. We ask: What is wrong with that? What is wrong with the public being involved in developing our economy and using the wealth that is generated to provide a better life for everyone? For our part, we support that principle. We feel that the Government is not doing that, but we support the principle.
The Hon. Member also talked about Crown corporations distorting the marketplace. He made a rather incredible statement which implied that he still believed in Adam Smith's myth of the invisible hand. He does not seem to recognize that the marketplace in today's world is manipulated by giant corporations, that we live in a world of administered prices, and that large corporate takeovers have absolutely nothing to do with the concept of the invisible hand.
We want to see Crown corporations made accountable, because too often they act like other corporations in our society; they end up serving their own interests rather than the public interest. They end up serving Liberal Party patronage rather than the public interest. We find in our constituencies that many people are frustrated and fed up with large impersonal systems and corporations which operate in a blind manner so that ordinary people cannot seem to get a handle on them. Even the management of some of these large systems do not seem to be really in control. We suggest that Crown corporations offer the possibility of an alternative model which could be open, accountable and could serve community purposes. Instead, we have the kind of arrogance typified by de Havilland which has incurred large debts, which have been followed by bail-outs and lay-offs and, incredible as it might seem, by bonuses paid to members of the executive.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) pointed out last week that de Havilland has top-heavy management. For example, in 1981 there were 3,500 employees on the shop floor and 1,900 management employees. In 1984,
Financial Administration Act
there are 1,300 floor employees and 1,400 management employees. There is a slush fund for management retirees and nothing for the workers except lay-offs.
I received a letter from a constituent who was very concerned because he is fighting to keep a small business operating, at a time when de Havilland is giving bonuses to executives who have lost money.

Mr. Speaker, many Members of this House have had experience in committee with executives of Crown corporations and with the Ministers responsible in this House for Crown corporations. We find that in many cases Crown corporations are not answerable to the House or to parliamentary committee and, I dare say, in most cases are not even answerable to the Government. This Bill is at best a feeble attempt to try to address that issue. However, Mr. Speaker, I say that Bill C-24 does not go far enough.
The Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) believes philosophically that the more Crown corporations you have, the better for the economy. I do not subscribe to that viewpoint. When one examines the amount of money that is generated by Canadians in goods and services and the percentage of those goods and services which are taken by governments at all levels, one sees that we have moved well beyond a mixed economy and are moving dangerously close to the point where government will be the chief architect of the direction and planning of the economy. He will recall that the CNR actually grew out of a number of private railway corporations which were created in the second phase of railway development, especially in western Canada. I know the same thing applies to the CPR, but I constantly hear the NDP raising the point that Crown corporations can deal with the conditions of the marketplace as well as turn a profit. However, in most cases the evidence is directly opposite. Therefore, if there is not a social

Mr. Speaker, in speaking on Bill C-24 my thoughts go back a number of years to the period in time when we were dealing with AECL. At that particular time, one of the members of the committee decided to ask Government officials exactly how many Crown corporations the Canadian Government had control of. The answer to the first question was that it was in the vicinity of 100 or so. Day after day those officials kept coming back for further questions. Every day they came back they had a few more Crown corporations. They were embarrassed. The more Crown corporations they had to announce to the committee, the more embarrassed they were. I would think that today any responsible Government would be terribly embarrassed to count the number of Crown corporations that the Canadian Government has to service 25 million people. After all, Mr. Speaker, what are Crown corporations for? They are not there for their own purposes but, rather, to give service to the people. We now see that the whole system is getting out of control, to the point where it will be a horrendous task for any government to regain control of the Crown corporation system in Canada. Crown corporations are multiplying like rabbits.
Eventually, the sunset clause with regard to any legislation must be reinstated so that legislation can be brought back to Parliament and sustained for the benefit of the people in Canada. Otherwise, the entire system will get completely out of control. This is what has happened to government officials who have attempted to determine the number of Crown corporations that exist in Canada. I do not think that anyone really knows what the number is today as a result of subsidiaries multiplying so quickly.
Let us consider Petro-Canada, which was supposed to be a window on the industry. The House will recall what the then Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said at the time,
May 8, 1984

that this was the reason this corporation was being established. It was primarily because the Leader of the NDP at the time, Mr. David Lewis, was harping on the subject of corporate welfare bums. Canadians finally became upset about this and decided that perhaps there was something taking place of which they were not aware. However, I maintain that it is not necessary to have a Crown corporation in order to have a window on an industry. That is the responsibility of the Government. We have the vehicle available to us to be able to delve into those situations and determine whether an individual or corporation is making excess profits. This can be dealt with accordingly through the taxation structure.
Instead, the government of the day decided to set up a so-called window on the industry. Some window! According to the latest figures I have, Petro-Canada has 54 subsidiaries under its control. That is how quickly it has multiplied since its inception.
Let me quote from a statement made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) to the Ottawa Citizen. He said, "Petro-Canada's latest spending spree, its partial takeover of BP Canada Limited", British Petroleum Canada Limited, "for $347 million is simply a good commercial deal". I suggest that the Hon. Minister made a mistake. The Government did not really want to have a window on the industry. What it wanted was to get into the oil business. We now find that Petro-Canada wants to sell off 400 of its service stations in eastern Canada because it does not have any use for them and they are making it go broke.
If Petro-Canada had to operate within the same structure as does any private corporate entity, it would have gone bankrupt long ago. Hundreds of millions of dollars have gone into Petro-Canada to buy Petrofina and then BP. All of the interest was paid for out of the revolving term loan of the Canadian ownership account. It must be great to have a sugar daddy like that, and I am sure that William Hopper is delighted to be fed cash to enable him to continue paying those debts. He must be pleased that he does not have to show his debt equity relationship.
The facts would come out if we had appropriate legislation. This is why the Government must be held accountable for the Crown corporation legislation. We cannot allow the current situation to continue because it will bankrupt us.
I stand to be corrected but I believe that Mr. Hopper is the director of some 23 subsidiaries that are related to Petro-Canada. The latest figure also shows that Petro-Canada has at least 6,900 person years. This massive corporation is just one example of the Crown corporations with which we must cope. Canadians in the future will face havoc if the Government continues to get itself into this dilemma by promoting Crown corporations without having any sunset clauses.
Let us examine Canagrex, one of the most recent Crown corporations. It was brought in by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). I have talked to people within the Department of Supply and Services who were satisfied that they had all the necessary facilities to accommodate the export industry that Canagrex could possibly generate. Such duplication of services
Adjournment Motion
only causes an overlap, which is a major cause of problems for our country. There is too much overlap between departments of federal, provincial and municipal governments, which only creates much frustration.
For example, when two or three corporations are involved in a single project, one cannot make a decision and accomplish something without the approval of the others. This is a situation that is taking place in the country today. It also happens between the federal and provincial governments. For example, it was reported several years ago that there were 600 meetings between the federal Government and the provincial Government of Alberta alone at the ministerial level, employee level and throughout the system. This is what people mean when they talk about a heavy government overburden on the taxpayers. This duplication and overlapping of services must not continue.
I know that I am expressing the opinion of 100 per cent of my constituents as their Member of Parliament in the House of Commons when I say that they would be very happy if the Government were to take the opposite approach and cut down on the number of Crown corporations and the overburden of Government that has been allowed to take place in Canada. Only then will we be able to create a situation in which the taxpayers will be able to carry the load that the Government thrusts upon them.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to take part in this debate on Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof.
In looking at this Bill, we find that it is virtually a skeleton Bill because most of what will really happen concerning the Government's intentions on Crown corporations will depend on regulations which have not yet been drafted.
We have rejected this unparliamentary approach to legislation so many times in the past that it is hardly worth-while wasting one's breath or devoting a lot of time to it now. Needless to say, this Bill attempts woefully, I suggest, to deal with a problem which is crying out for meaningful reform. All this Bill contains is cosmetic changes that will do nothing to revamp any Crown corporation meaningfully.
The Minister states that Bill C-24 is designed to strengthen the control and accountability of Crown corporations. However, he neglected to tell us that the Bill does not affect all Crown corporations. There are now some 315 Crown corporations under federal jurisdiction, but this Bill, woefully, will deal with only 183. Really, Mr. Speaker, any child can see that this Bill does not come to grips with and does not accomplish what the Government promises. It really does nothing to strengthen the control and accountability of Crown corporations. There is really no comprehensive plan of action to deal with an extremely serious situation. This Bill could have provided the opportunity for a long awaited and necessary reform in an area that is in great need of meaningful changes. But simply put, Mr. Speaker, it does not do the job that it sets out to do.
I am not going to deal with specific examples of the inadequacies of Crown corporations because we have too many examples of this already in the record enunciated by many speakers in the debate. The record of Crown corporations in Canada is anything but good. Very few of them ever show a profit. In fact, last year they lost a total of some $4 billion, which is underwritten by you and me, the Canadian taxpayers. Crown corporations are good examples of why governments should not be involved in business. I grant you that there may be a few essential areas where government must be involved, but really, Mr. Speaker, 315 Crown corporations? That is ridiculous. If this Bill is to be passed eventually, Mr. Speaker,
it should be amended, completely overhauled and completely restructured if it is to do the job and do it properly.
It seems to me that in Bill C-24 the Government is trying to have itself perceived by the people of Canada, and is trying to convince Canadians of it in the Bill, as having Finally gained control over Crown corporations. Crown corporations have been totally uncontrolled for many years, running their own show and oblivious of the fact that they are responsible to the people of Canada. Unfortunately, gaining control over Crown corporations with Bill C-24 is just an illusion and nothing more. It is a bluff by the Government that will not go unnoticed by Canadians. With this Government, Mr. Speaker, government by Order in Council has become a way of life and Parliament has been turned into a rubberstamping organization. That is why we have Bills such as this before us. That is why this Bill gives all the power over Crown corporations not to Parliament, but to the Cabinet. Only rarely does this Government really seek the approval of Parliament when it comes to the expenditure of taxpayers' dollars. That is why we are looking for accountability in this Bill.
There are many deficiencies in this Bill. This Bill shies away from presenting policy on matters of internal government organization. There is no reference to the privileges and immunities of Crown corporations. The Bill does not specify whether or not public servants may sit on the boards of Crown corporations. This Bill sidesteps the suggestion that a parliamentary overseeing committee should monitor Crown corporations. If this were done, Mr. Speaker, the Government could easily avoid the threat of cover-up accusations. It is common sense that if all Parties are involved, there is bound to be less suspicion of underhanded tactics on the part of the Government or Cabinet.
It is our hope to have the opportunity to make amendments to this Bill, which would institute the necessary checks and balances to prevent the Government from running wild. What Bill C-24 now presents nowhere near gives the answers that all Canadians would like to see in bringing some semblance of control over and accountability to Crown corporations. Let us hope that the necessary changes will be made to Bill C-24 that will result in a meaningful Bill, one which it will be possible for all Members of all Parties in the House to support in order to bring Crown corporations at long last under the control of the representatives of Canada's taxpayers.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations. I must say that in listening today to the various speakers I could not help but think of the individual who purchases a bag of apples from the store and, because there is a bad apple somewhere in the bag, takes the whole bag and throws it out. I have listened to speaker after speaker this afternoon, mainly Conservatives, saying how horrible Crown corporations are and how they have failed to serve the people of Canada. I cannot help but think of the eight Conservative Governments that exist across the country and, in terms of total assets, have more in Crown corporations than

the federal Government has altogether. I do not understand in a sense the theme of the criticism-

As the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) says, maybe there is some ring of hypocrisy in the comments. However, I will not say that necessarily, Mr. Speaker. One of the very earliest Crown corporations in this part of the world, in central Canada, goes back to 1906 when the Conservative Government in the Province of Ontario decided that a Crown corporation should have a monopoly over all the power generated in the Province of Ontario and that that was in the best interests of the citizens of Ontario. The Government essentially established Ontario Hydro at that time. Because of the obvious advantage, I suppose, in having a Crown corporation responsible for such a critical energy resource, we saw similar things in British Columbia under the Social Credit Government, again the establishment of a Crown corporation to oversee hydro developments. There were similar acts across the country. I suppose that one of the most recent was the Conservative Government takeover of Pacific Western Airlines a little while ago, again in the best interests of Western Canadians, as Premier Lougheed said at that time. It was said that the service being provided by the private airline was not adequately serving Western Canadians, at least in the mind of the Premier of Alberta. He decided that PWA should become a Crown corporation.
One could go on and on, Mr. Speaker, and list literally hundreds of Crown corporations that Conservative governments, as well as Liberal and Social Credit governments, have created for one reason or another in the best interest, at the time of creation, of the citizens of a province or, as far as the federal Government was concerned, in the best interest of the people of Canada.
The tradition of Crown corporations is as Canadian as the beaver or the hockey stick. Crown corporations have been part of the economic fabric of the Canadian economy virtually since their inception. I refer to the origin of Crown corporations which goes back to 1841 when the joint Governments of Upper and Lower Canada decided, in the best interest of Canada at that time, that an integrated canal system would benefit Canadians. The Governments of Upper and Lower Canada got together and established a board, which was essentially the forerunner of Crown corporations in the transportation industry. Most recently, of course, and the most obvious is the creation of the Canadian National Railways, again created by and large in an effort to bail out some financially pressed transportation companies, three railroad companies that had grown up at the second stage of the railroad era in Canada and which found themselves in financial difficulties. Because the Government of the day felt it was appropriate that these rail lines be maintained, that the service they provided and the development, particularly of western Canada, was very important, the creation of the CNR as a Crown corporation took place. Since then, Mr. Speaker, we
Financial Administration Act
have seen many other examples of Crown corporations created to serve Canadians in one way or another.
While I do not want for a moment to suggest that the Bill before us is adequate, that the Bill before us will resolve the problems attached to Crown corporations, I will say that it is at least a step in the right direction. What we have found in Crown corporations is that while certain areas might have been nationalized, they have not been socialized. While Crown corporations are intended to represent the views of Canadian society and to reflect social and economic policy, in more cases than not they act no different from their corporate brothers in the private sector. Their motives seem to be profits only. Their motives appear to be the shareholders, in this case the people of Canada, as opposed to being an arm or a vehicle with which to develop economic policy in the best interests of Canada.
I should like to refer to some Crown corporations which tend to be glossed over in the criticisms Hon. Members have raised in the last number of days. I refer to corporations such as the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety, the Medical Research Council, the National Museums of Canada, the National Research Council of Canada, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, the Science Council of Canada, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, the Canada Council, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the Farm Credit Corporation, the Export Development Corporation, and Teleglobe Canada. One could go on and on listing Crown corporations, which are not perfect by a long shot but which provide a very valuable service to Canadians.
First, I will refer to the Export Development Corporation. In what position would Canadian exporters be today, in what position would Canadian firms be today, if they did not have an organization like the Export Development Corporation standing behind them to assist in ensuring for their commodities, as they move into overseas ports, some type of supportive financing? In every exporting country in the world today, there are Crown corporations providing that kind of supportive system, the type of financial support needed to compete on international markets in today's competitive world.
I do not understand the critics of this particular Bill. I do not know whether or not the Conservatives would like to do away with the Export Development Corporation. Are they saying that we should do away with the Farm Credit Corporation? It is not perfectly clear, and I do not want to put words into their mouths. While there is a great deal of room for criticism, let us not throw out the baby with the bath water or throw out the whole bushel of apples because one or two are a little rotten or sour.
It has become perfectly clear that Bill C-24 does not go far enough. It is inadequate. When we lump Canadair and Canada Council in the same Bill and say that they are to be approached in a similar way, it misses the point as to how different are those two Crown corporations. For example, it is

May 8, 1984
Financial Administration Act
imperative that Canada Council remain at arm's length from this institution. When Prime Minister Louis St. Laurent brought in the Canada Council Act, the point he made was that it was important for Canada to encourage the development of the cultural arts at arms length, not to control the development of the arts in Canada. That distinction is very important.
When it comes to accountability, I sat through the sessions when Canadair appeared before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, only to hear those corporate directors misrepresent and mislead. I would not go so far as to say that they would lie to us, but they certainly misrepresented the information they were presenting. They refused to tell us all sorts of points when specific questions were put to them.
If they are to be accountable, this Bill before us must be altered. While we have a tendency to support the concept of this Bill, the principle of Crown corporations, we certainly have grave reservations about it in its existing form and will certainly be suggesting amendments at the appropriate stage.
